newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - June 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - June 27.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents.
-- WINDFALL TAX WILL RAISE OVER FIVE BLN STG

Latest figures from the British government reveal that proceeds from the windfall tax will be about two billion stg higher than the government has set aside for its welfare-to-work programme, at a total of about five billion stg. Senior members of the government state that chancellor Gordon Brown is continuing to resist pressure to drop the proposed 20 percent tax credit on dividends when the Budget is released next week. British Telecom will make the biggest individual contribution, to the windfall tax, at about one billion stg.
-- US COURT STRIKES DOWN LAW OVER 'PORN' ON INTERNET

In a landmark decision, the US Supreme Court has stricken down the Community Decency Act (CDA) passed by Congress last year, claiming it restricted free speech rights protected by the first amendment. The CDA had called for severe restrictions on the distribution of 'indecent' material on the Internet to protect children, but Supreme Court Justice John Paul Stevens declared the CDA also suppressed 'a large amount of free speech that adults have a constitutional right to receive and address to one another', noting the vagueness of the terms 'indecent' and 'offensive' which could have applied to non-pornographic, educational material.
-- WATER GROUPS URGED TO MAKE ONE-OFF PRICE CUT

Water industry regulator Ian Byatt has increased pressure on water companies to scale down dividend payouts and make a one-off price cut at the next review of charges in 1999. While Byatt would not speculate on the financial impact of his decision, UBS research has suggested that the one-off cut could result in a reduction of 10-15 stg in the average domestic bill.
The Water Services Association trade body has welcomed the move, but warned future prices must depend on investment obligations.
-- RAILTRACK GIVES IN TO REGULATOR

In an effort to avoid confrontation with rail regulator John Swift, Railtrack has promised to modify its operating licence to allow rail industry regulator OFRAIL greater power to monitor its performance. Deputy prime minister John Prescott commented that the deal served to demonstrate weaknesses in the rail regulator's regime.
-- HEALTH GROUPS WARNED OFF TOBACCO ACTION

UK minister for Health Tessa Jowell has warned off health authorities in the country of taking up legal actions against the tobacco industry, following the recent multi-billion US settlement. The NHS Confederation has unanimously agreed to set up a working group to 'consider the potential contribution of the tobacco companies of the costs to the NHS of smoking-related diseases' and will be 'keeping a tight rein' on health authorities.
-- LOTTERY REGULATOR SEEKS POWERS TO FINE CAMELOT

The director-general of UK lottery watchdog Oflot, Peter Davis, has once again begun lobbying for the right to impose heavy, 'meaningful' fines on National Lottery organisers Camelot Group Plc LOTT.CN for breaches of licence. Davis continues to maintain Camelot has failed to allow enough retail outlets to sell lottery tickets, but until now, his only option was to consider seeking a High Court injunction against the company.
-- LONRHO TO STEP UP ON DISPOSALS

With prospects for its three billion stg merger with South African fading, Lonrho Plc, the conglomerate, has made plans to increase its rate of disposals. As part of Lonrho's reshaping, 60 million stg will be raised through the sale of its 70 percent stake in US exploration and production company Hondo Oil & Gas. The group is also in talks with the Zimbabwe government, which has been seeking to acquire a 'significant' stake in its gold mining and ranching operations there.
-- NORWAY'S STATOIL IN 415 MLN STG NORTH SEA ASSET SWAP DEALS

State-owned Norwegian oil company Statoil has streamlined its North Sea oil and gas interests through a series of asset swaps with British Petroleum, Chevron, Elf, Total and Norsk Hydro worth upwards of 415 million stg. The series of deals will result in the change of ownership of 340 million barrels of oil and 36.5 billion cubic metres of natural gas. Analysts believe the swaps were made as part of the company's strategy to reposition itself.
-- SIGNET REBELS TO PRESS FOR REVIEW

Upset at shareholder approval for a capital reconstruction at the jewelry retailer, rebel Signet investors from UK Active Value Fund are seeking to break up the group. UKAV are planning to hold a meeting with the Signet board to press for a 'strategic review' of Signet, including the sale of its UK business and the flotation of the US arm. James McAdam, Signet's chairman insists that 'no part of Signet is up for sale'.
-- SHARES IN HAMLET PLUNGE 45 PERCENT ON WARNING

Following a profit warning from clothing group Hamlet Group Plc that figures for the year to June would be 'very substantially' below expectations, shares in the company fell 45 percent to their lowest levels since the group's flotation four years ago.
